newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Bolivian official says tin privatization at risk.
newsitem.headline: Bolivian official says tin privatization at risk.

text.p: A conflict at Bolivia's biggest tin mine is putting Thursday's planned privatization of the Empresa Metalurgica Vinto tin smelter at risk, the government said Wednesday.

"This sort of attitude definitely frightens those who were interested in (buying) Vinto," Mining Secretary Teddy Cuentas told reporters. He added that the Huanuni mine, 170 miles (270 km) south of La Paz, was nonetheless producing normally.
About 200 jobless workers occupied the Mount Posokini zone of Huanuni 10 days ago calling for small mine concessions.
But Cuentas repeated the government's refusal to meet the demands, adding that Posokini must be developed by big firms which will invest heavily and bring in modern technology.
The privatization of Vinto, which has the capacity to produce 30,000 tonnes a year of tin, is the last in the government's program of selling state assets.

Four companies were shortlisted last year to bid in the privatization tender for Vinto: Australia's Renison Goldfields Consolidated; Glencore International of Switzerland; Smelting Corp Berhad of Malaysia and Brazil's Paranapanema.
Apart from its Bolivian supplies from state-owned mines and small producers, Vinto also tolls tin concentrates from Peru's Minsur into metal.

The government plans to award 50 percent of Vinto to private hands, as well as administrative control. The other shares will be used to finance a new private pension fund system and divided among adult Bolivian citizens.
The winner of the tender will also be awarded control of the government's Huanuni and Colquiri tin mines.
